paras: The lynching of John Patton (also reported as John Potter) was the killing of a prisoner charged with horse stealing, who was taken from a deputy sheriff on the road near Kerrville, Texas, in May 1881 and shot dead. No one was identified, and the case reached papers outside Texas as an example of Texas "lawlessness".

Deputy Sheriff Clemens, described as of "Kerrville county" in the Texas report and of "Kimball county" in the wire version, had left San Antonio a few days earlier with two prisoners. Patton was charged with horse stealing and was on his way to be tried, and the second prisoner, William Dunman (printed "Durman" in Omaha), was charged with murder.

According to a letter from Kerrville summarized in a San Antonio special of May 13, the deputy was waylaid near Kerrville on the preceding Sunday by a party of men who stood in the middle of the road with drawn revolvers. The wire dispatch of May 16 put the spot about seventy miles west of San Antonio and the party at four men, who demanded the prisoners. The deputy yielded and, in the wire version, was told to go on a short distance and wait, after which he heard shots and later learned that Patton had been killed. The Texas report said simply that Potter was "shot down in the road" shortly after the prisoners were taken.

The men took the deputy's pistol and released Dunman. According to the wire, Dunman was told that Patton was shot for killing three children of a family named Doud, and that he himself was freed for "developing the facts while in prison with Patton"; this account of motive came only from the men themselves, as relayed.

The deputy reported the killing in town, and an inquest was held on the body. The Texas report stated that nothing was known of who the men were or of the object of the killing, and no report of arrests appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Daily Herald carried the story first, on May 14, in a column of San Antonio telegraph items under the headline "Prisoner Potter Shot to Death Near Laredo", although its own text placed the killing near Kerrville. Its brief account emphasized that the deputy "could do nothing but comply", and the Dallas Weekly Herald reprinted it on May 19.

Outside Texas, the San Antonio wire of May 16 ran in the Omaha Daily Bee under "TEXAS LAWLESSNESS", in a crime column beside an averted lynching in Michigan, and in the Savannah Morning News under "A MURDEROUS TEXAS MOB". None of the reports mentioned the race of the victim or of the men who killed him.

The reports differ on the victim's surname (Patton in the wire, Potter in the Texas special) and the deputy's county (Kimball or Kerrville), and the Texas special, drawn from a Kerrville letter, is the closer source on place. They also differ on motive: the Texas report called it unknown, while the wire relayed the men's claim that Patton had killed three children.

bases: A party of armed men took two prisoners from a deputy sheriff on the road and shot one of them dead (A1, A2, A3).

Four men (A2, A3), or 'a party of unknown men' (A1), took a prisoner charged with horse stealing from a deputy and shot him without any legal authority; according to the wire account the released prisoner was told Patton was shot for killing three children (A3), although the Texas report said the object of the killing was unknown (A1).

A San Antonio special based on a letter from Kerrville (A1) and a separate San Antonio wire dispatch of May 16 (A2, A3) agree that a deputy named Clemens was stopped on the road, his prisoners were taken, and the prisoner charged with horse stealing was shot dead.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald gave a short factual item under 'Prisoner Potter Shot to Death', stressing that the deputy 'could do nothing but comply' and that the motive was unknown.
The Omaha Bee ran the wire under 'TEXAS LAWLESSNESS' in a 'Record of Crime' column alongside murders and an averted Michigan lynching.
The Savannah Morning News headed the same wire 'A MURDEROUS TEXAS MOB'.
